01.r: Carries the story on to the manager's next step.

02.r: The manager summons the debtors to come to him.
02.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the middle voice, used here, means 'to call to oneself'. It is an aorist participle: the summons comes before the questioning.

03.r: With 'each', stresses that he dealt with them one at a time.

05.r: The article; 'of' comes from the genitive case.

06.r: Those who owed goods or money to the manager's master.
06.n: The same compound word as in Luke 7:41 on this page; Abbott-Smith explains it as χρέος, a debt, joined to ὀφειλέτης, a debtor, and lists these two verses as its only New Testament uses.

07.r: The article of the phrase 'of his own master'; 'of' comes from the case.

08.r: The master whose affairs the manager runs.
08.n: A human owner, so 'master' by this study's register. STEPBible tags this occurrence with the human sense.

09.n: A reflexive pronoun: 'his own'. It makes plain that these are debts owed to the master, not to the manager.

10.r: He puts the question to the first debtor.
10.n: The imperfect tense, literally 'he was saying'. Greek narrative often introduces speech this way, and English says simply 'he said'.

11.r: The article; 'to' comes from the dative case.

12.r: The first debtor to be called in.

13.r: Asks the size of the debt.
13.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse for the neuter used on its own, 'how much'.

14.r: The present tense: what the debtor still owes.
14.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse for the verb with the dative of the person owed: 'to owe to my master'.

15.r: The article of 'my master'; 'to' comes from the dative case.

16.r: The same master whose debtors these are.

17.r: The manager speaks of his master as his own.
